notes: \cpara{Sets up the example: an urn of seventy white and thirty red balls, from which you draw ten.}
\cpara{Shows random error: a sample of ten may give the right count or, by chance, a wrong one.}
\cpara{Says random error is right on average and shrinks as you learn more. Both are true of a random sample.}
\cpara{Introduces bias with one change: the heavier white balls sink, so samples lean toward red.}
\cpara{Defines statistical bias and draws the contrast with random error: more data may not help.}
\cpara{Draws the lesson: to be sure that learning more helps, we must find and correct the biases in our data.}

\cpara{Defines cognitive bias by analogy: a systematic error in how we think, as opposed to a random error or plain ignorance. The parenthesis widens it to thinking that ``less reliably serves our other goals.''}
\cpara{Illustrates with the urn: wanting the red balls to cure your brother leads you to overestimate how many there are.}
\cpara{Lists what the two kinds of bias share, and says debiasing is harder when the faulty instrument is yourself.}
\cpara{Argues that biases are the place to start, since trusting anything depends on trusting your brain.}

\cpara{Opens a version of Tversky and Kahneman's ``Steve'' problem (\textsc{Science}, 1974), cut down to one trait. Their Steve is ``very shy and withdrawn,'' with a longer description, and their list of occupations includes ``salesman'' and ``librarian.''}

\cpara{Gives the answer most people give and the base rate that makes it a mistake: salespeople are seventy-five times as common as librarians in the United States. The figure is sourced to a psychology textbook, which I could not check.}
\cpara{Names the error, base rate neglect, and adds a second bias, the sunk cost fallacy.}
\cpara{States the difficulty the book must meet: knowing about a bias neither protects you from it nor lets you notice it in action.}

\cpara{Reports Hansen et al. (2014) accurately. Participants were led to use a strategy they rated as biasing (seeing the painter's name before judging), were biased by it, and afterward ``claimed more objectivity than they had prior to using the strategy.''}

\cpara{Adds the bias blind spot: people see bias in others more readily than in themselves, and read the absence of ``biased-feeling thoughts'' as the absence of bias. I did not check the two studies cited.}
\cpara{The turn of the argument: biases can be overcome, though ``It's just not trivial.'' The only evidence given is one sentence, without a source, about thinking of probabilities as frequencies.}

\cpara{States the book's method and its support. The support is a comparison, made conditional (``To the extent this volume does its job''), with Serfas's finding that accounting courses reduced sunk-cost bias and work experience did not. Accounting courses are formal instruction in a subject; the book is a collection of blog essays. The introduction gives no evidence that reading them has the effect the courses had.}

\clogic{This is an approach through understanding. It sits uneasily with the Preface, a few pages earlier, which calls Yudkowsky's largest mistake not seeing that ``the big problem in learning this valuable way of thinking was figuring out how to practice it, not knowing the theory.''}

\cpara{Quotes Serfas: expertise needs an understanding of a bias's rationale, the ability ``to spot it in the particular setting,'' and ``the appropriate tools at hand to counteract the bias.'' The book's stated approach, understanding, is the first of these three. I could not check the quotation against Serfas's book.}
\cpara{States the goal: rationality ``expertise,'' meaning a deep understanding of human bias and self-deception.}
\cpara{Gives the book's origin: Yudkowsky's essays of 2006 to 2009, grouped into sequences and then into six books.}
\cpara{Describes the style as personal and irreverent, and links it to Yudkowsky's \textsc{Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality}.}
\cpara{Credits the book's organizing idea to Korzybski. The quotation matches the one Wikipedia gives from \textsc{Science and Sanity} (1933), p.~58.}
\cpara{Names the book's four sequences and its closing dialogue, ``The Simple Truth.''}
\cpara{Ends with Dan Ariely's phrase ``predictably irrational'' and the hope that understanding our errors can help us build a better future.}
